prompt: Write a note to a friend about lessons from rebuilding a service people depend on every day. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the note only.
final_message:
Hey Sam,

You asked how the rebuild went, so here's the honest version. I've been chewing on it for weeks.

First, the boring service is the dangerous one. Nobody thanks you for the thing that works every morning, which means nobody can tell you what it quietly does. We found behaviors no one had written down: a retry that papered over a flaky upstream, a sort order a partner's script relied on, a timeout that happened to be forgiving. The old system had a thousand small promises, and we only learned them by breaking them. If I did it again, I'd spend the first month just documenting what the current system really does, not what the spec says it does.

Second, run old and new side by side for longer than feels reasonable. We shadowed live traffic and compared outputs, and the diffs were humbling. Most were our bugs, but a handful were the old system being wrong in ways people had adapted to. Deciding whether to preserve a bug is a real product decision, and it deserves a real owner, not whoever is on call.

Third, migrate in slices. Moving one small group of users at a time felt slow, but every rollback was cheap and every surprise was small. The one time we got impatient and widened a rollout early, we spent a weekend regretting it.

Fourth, be boringly clear with the people depending on you. We told users what was changing, when, and how to reach us. Fewer complaints came from the changes themselves than from people feeling blindsided. A short, plain heads-up beat any clever feature.

Fifth, protect the team. Rebuilds drag on, and morale sags around month four when the new thing still isn't finished and the old thing still needs care. Celebrating small milestones sounds corny, but it kept us going.

The biggest surprise is that the hard part wasn't technical. It was restraint: not adding features, not "fixing" things that weren't in scope, and resisting the urge to make the new system impressive instead of faithful. We got to be impressive later, once trust was banked.

If you're thinking of doing something similar, I'm happy to share our checklists and the mistakes in more detail. Coffee soon?
